standard.title: Causes of WWI and Australian Enlistment
standard.description: the causes of the First World War and the reasons why Australians enlisted to fight in the war
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied Australian colonial development and Federation. They understand European imperial expansion (AC9HH9K01) and Australia's development in relation to the world by 1914 (AC9HH9K07). They have not yet systematically studied the causes of the First World War or the mechanisms of imperial alliance systems. They have some general awareness of WWI from prior schooling but have not analytically examined its causes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and describe the causes of the First World War and explain the reasons why Australians enlisted to fight.

nodes.label: Long-term causes — MAIN
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the long-term structural causes of WWI including militarism, the alliance system, imperialism, and nationalism.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least two long-term causes of WWI.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe the four long-term causes (MAIN): Militarism (arms race, military culture), Alliance System (Triple Entente vs Triple Alliance), Imperialism (competition for colonies, economic rivalry), Nationalism (ethnic nationalism, pressure on multi-ethnic empires like Austria-Hungary); explain how these causes created a fragile, interconnected European order prone to rapid escalation.
wider: Investigate the arms race between Britain and Germany as a concrete example of militarism — examining naval rivalry and the Dreadnought programme as factors that increased the probability of conflict

Examine how nationalism operated as both a unifying and destabilising force — including how it strengthened nation-states while simultaneously threatening multi-ethnic empires like Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire
Investigate how imperial competition in Africa and Asia in the early 20th century created friction between European powers — examining the Moroccan Crises as near-war moments before 1914
nodes.hinge_reason: The MAIN causes provide the structural explanation for why war was possible. Without understanding these, students will reduce WWI to 'the assassination' — missing the underlying conditions that made a single event trigger a world war. All subsequent analysis of the war's significance depends on understanding why it happened.

response_modes.reason: Students need an explicit framework (MAIN) before engaging with specific examples — the categories help organise what would otherwise be a disconnected list of historical facts. Model how each cause type works before asking students to apply it.

success_criteria: Identifies and describes all four MAIN long-term causes of WWI
Explains how at least two causes interacted to create conditions for large-scale conflict

nodes.label: Short-term triggers and the outbreak of war
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the short-term triggers of WWI including the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the July Crisis, and Germany's invasion of Belgium.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and explain how it triggered the outbreak of war.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe the short-term triggers: the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (June 1914); the July Crisis — Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia, mobilisation and alliance chain reactions; Germany's invasion of Belgium and Britain's entry; explain how these triggers activated the alliance systems built over preceding decades.
wider: Examine the July Crisis in detail — tracking the diplomatic decisions made by each major power in the weeks after the assassination — to assess whether war was inevitable or whether different choices could have prevented it
Investigate Germany's Schlieffen Plan and how its rigid military timetables constrained diplomatic options once mobilisation began — examining how military planning shaped political outcomes

Compare how different nations experienced the outbreak of war (e.g. Germany, France, Britain, Serbia, Australia) to examine how the 'short-term trigger' was experienced differently depending on national position

response_modes.reason: The sequence of events in July-August 1914 is specific and needs accurate recall — assassination → ultimatum → mobilisation → alliance chain → Britain's entry — before students can use it analytically.

success_criteria: Describes the assassination and its immediate political consequences
Explains how the alliance system caused a localised crisis to escalate into a world war

nodes.label: Australian responses and reasons for enlistment
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the different perspectives toward war in 1914, examine Australian political leaders' responses, and describe the range of reasons why Australians enlisted.
nodes.minimum_width: List at least three distinct reasons why Australian men enlisted in the AIF.
nodes.typical_width: Explain different perspectives toward war at the turn of the 20th century (war as noble/heroic, as adventure, and sceptical views); examine Australian political leaders' responses (e.g. Fisher's 'last man and last shilling' pledge); describe the range of enlistment motivations including duty to the British Empire, adventure, economic reasons, propaganda, peer pressure; examine the stories of First Nations Australian men who enlisted.
wider: Examine the experiences of First Nations Australian men who enlisted — including the barriers they faced in being accepted, their service conditions, and how their service was recognised or ignored — to assess how imperial loyalty coexisted with racial exclusion
Analyse WWI recruitment propaganda (posters, pamphlets, speeches) as primary sources — identifying the range of persuasive appeals used and assessing their effectiveness
Compare the motivations of Australian volunteers with those of conscripted soldiers from other Allied nations — assessing how voluntarism shaped the Australian wartime experience differently

response_modes.reason: The range of enlistment motivations — from genuine imperial loyalty to economic desperation to peer pressure — should be examined across multiple social groups, not flattened to a single type.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Australian enlistment motivations reveal a complex picture of imperial identity, masculinity, economic vulnerability, and social pressure. The First Nations enlistment story is particularly rich — involving both loyalty to country and willingness to fight for a nation that had denied them citizenship rights.
success_criteria: Describes at least four distinct reasons why Australians enlisted, across different motivational categories
Explains at least one way Australian political responses to the outbreak of war reflected Australia's relationship with the British Empire
